query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored post-solidification heat treatment—with an optimized isothermal hold followed by rapid quenching—will induce nanoscale precipitate formation at the internal boundaries of eutectic high-entropy alloys, thereby strengthening these interfaces and simultaneously improving both room-temperature tensile strength and ductility compared to conventional as-cast samples.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloys exhibiting dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries that are prone to microcrack initiation under tensile loading.
generation.intervention: A tailored annealing schedule consisting of an isothermal hold at a specific temperature (to allow controlled nucleation of nanoscale precipitates) followed by rapid quenching.
generation.conditions: The treatment should be applied after solidification on alloys with a precise eutectic composition. The isothermal hold temperature and time must be selected to promote nucleation of nanoscale precipitates at the colony interfaces without causing precipitate coarsening, followed by a sufficiently rapid cooling rate to freeze the beneficial microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale precipitates that form along the internal boundaries of the lamellar colonies.
generation.mechanism: The formation of these nanoscale precipitates enhances the cohesion of the internal boundaries, impeding stress concentration and dislocation pile-up. This reduces microcrack initiation during tensile loading, thereby simultaneously improving strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy will exhibit higher tensile strength and increased ductility at room temperature relative to the untreated (as-cast) baseline, due to improved interfacial integrity and mitigated microcracking.
generation.baseline: Conventional processing of the eutectic high-entropy alloy (as-cast condition) that results in dual-phase lamellar colonies with unmodified internal boundaries prone to microcracking.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the heat treatment is contingent on the specific alloy composition and the precise control over annealing temperature, hold duration, and cooling rate. Deviations from the optimal processing window may lead to insufficient precipitate formation or undesirable coarsening.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements in strength and ductility, as well as the optimal processing parameters (temperature, duration, and quench rate) for achieving the desired nano-precipitate distribution, remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of eutectic high-entropy alloy specimens: one set processed by conventional casting (control) and another set subjected to the proposed tailored heat treatment (isothermal hold followed by rapid quenching). Both sets should be produced from the same alloy composition under identical casting conditions. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests and perform detailed microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM, SEM) to assess nanoscale precipitate formation at the lamellar boundaries.
measurements: Microstructural analysis confirming the presence, size, and distribution of nanoscale precipitates at internal boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated specimens do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the control group, or if the microstructural analyses do not confirm the formation of nanoscale precipitates at the internal boundaries, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Materials with high performance both at room and elevated temperatures are very attractive for a wide range of critical applications, potentially for aero-engine and fusion reactors [1] – [4] . For decades, ultra-strong, ductile, and heat-resistant materials have long been sought by the materials community, such as tungsten-based heavy alloys and nickel-based superalloys [3] , [5] . However, achieving alloys with an ultrahigh strength (>2 GPa) and a sufficient ductility (>10%) has presented a long-standing challenge. This has spurred significant research into metallurgical strategies to tailor microstructures for improved properties. One classical design paradigm is utilizing dilute concentrations of alloying elements, such as Re, Ti, and Cr, to improve the properties of W-based alloys; however, the “strength-ductility trade-off” has proven to be difficult to be solved with such single principal-element alloy systems due to the problem of brittle W-enriched phases with body-centered cubic (bcc) structures [5] , [6] . High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Even in such a bulk cast ingot, a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure characteristic of eutectic alloys was achieved. The inter-lamellar spacing was about 2 μm. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] .
